So tell me about your story, Red Rock.
And you know, obviously I read about it on the website, but read the presentation I'm provided.
Just want to hear your story and kind of where you're at and what big picture, what you're.
What you're hoping to accomplish with potentially selling the agency.

Well, it began, I guess, in retail, and that's where I understood the impact of visual and merchandising and store design and the impact that you could have on human behavior just within the bricks and mortar of retail.
But I saw the decline of retail as a category coming up, so I thought it best to transfer into more of a digital environment, but still apply that same interest of human psychology and.
But not so much pointing towards people to buy more stuff, but to use the skills that I'd acquired to do the work that needs to be done in this world.
And, you know, my sister was a doctor and she did her masters of public health at Boston and Harvard years ago.
So I've sort of been following her career a little bit and inspired by the work she's been doing, that's become more and more active in terms of public health outcomes.
So when I took the plunge to start red Rock in 25th, 2010, the Health and wellness community was my initial target.
And we were living in New Haven, obviously in Yale's backyard.

We were, we started working with Yale on a few different campaigns, and that led to working with Tulane University and Columbia University and more recently with a similar campaign in Michigan, and we're about to start another one in Atlanta.
And so our agency's reputation is quite well established in public health environment, and I've really, really enjoyed having measurable impact in that category.
Just between you and me, I really don't like the function of marketing, as in selling stuff.
I don't think people like to be sold to.
So hence the name Red Rock Branding.
And it's intentional to say that we're not a marketing organization.
We're more of a communications and community building function.
That's how we serve our clients in the most meaningful way.

And that's so much fun when you sort of delink those two, it becomes much more an authentic activity, but using all of the latest digital tools, of course, that I acquired when I was working with Fortune 500 companies.
So, yeah, our reputation is established there.
And as you know, recently the current administration has been quite aggressively chopping down those budgets.
So we've realized that we have a bit of a vulnerability as an agency towards public health.
So I guess one of the biggest challenges that I've had this year is just sort of rebalancing our client portfolio to be not just public health, but also in the green tech and blue tech spaces.
So we've got a fairly robust campaign that's going to roll out next week, actively seeking more clients in that space just to sort of balance out portfolio.
Because at the moment it's too, it's too biased towards public health.
And that, you know, from a financial point of view, I think that those funds will come back.
I'm just not sure when because, you know, earlier this year we lost two clients.
They were operating on the ARPA funding and they just had to stop immediately.
So we took a bit of a hit there.
But, you know, there's always market conditions that are out of your control.
So we'll, we'll see what happens.
But, you know, I.
And just to answer the other half of your question about, you know, my journey.
I'm more, more excited about this work now than I've ever been.
And it, it seems to be in an accumulative exercise when you get recognition and awards for the work you do that there's becomes a sort of an obligation to continue that.
Right.
So you've got a certain inertia, you know, go with it.
You'd be foolish not to.
So, so I am interested in, in talking about, you know, acquisition of some sort.
But I also, I'm also committed to making sure that the integrity of that work continues somehow.
And which is why I'm interested in your brand because there's clearly a lot of shared values because I've built a team that is very much excited about this work.
It makes us want to get up in the morning and sleep well at night and having that.
There's not many people in marketing business that can say that about the work they do, I find.
Absolutely, yes.
That's kind of what's kept us going as well.

And, and like you said, I think the specialization and the niche and building relationships and reputation within that niche is it, you know, often entails short term sacrifices because you're messing up those opportunities that might be lucrative but not aligned with the mission.
And then sometimes funding does get c cuts, you know, periods of cuts, but like you said, it does tend to rebound.
And the important thing is just to stay in the game.
And we've gone through that, of course, and as you probably saw on our website, I mean we've done.
Public health is one of our passions.
We started out really quite a while back in 2002 by being one of three agencies that got selected to be agency of record for the Texas Department of Health.

And so we got to work for about six or seven years on all the statewide immunization campaigns, on smoking cessation and prevention campaigns, a lot of behavior change campaigns, a lot of great research driven work where we would identify, you know, what were the obstacles to behavior change, what were the triggers that might get people to adopt lifestyle changes and make healthier choices.

And then after that, around the time that you were, you mentioned you started your firm was kind of a great time for public health because we had started doing work in like healthy nutrition and like physical activity.
And that was kind of the era of the Obama's work promoting the let's Move campaign.
There was some great funding around the country for, you know, these areas of healthy eating and physical activity.

We did a lot of work in that area and then we kind of got into the area of reduction of the consumption of sugary beverages and how sugary beverages contribute to chronic disease, diabetes and so forth.
So public health has just been something, you know, we're very, very passionate about.

And that was another thing that obviously really spoke to me about your agency, which is, you know, you guys have done co published or co written, published studies with some of your clients, I think I read.
And I mean, we've done the same.

So it just seems like a very rare, it's not very common, I think, in our, in our industry for agencies to get that deep into the work and really have a team that can, that can do that and that can kind of, you know, collaborate with PhDs and researchers at universities to make these things, to bring these things to life, you know, to learn, learn from them and then to improve the messaging and improve the campaigns.
So I definitely saw some synergy there, you know, for sure, I find that very appealing.
And the, the green tech and environmental area that you are also working, working in, we haven't done too much work in that field.

We have done a lot of work in kind of water quality and water conservation for like public utilities and water systems, you know, trying to get their communities to save water or to learn about ways to protect the quality of the, of the water supply through their, through their behavior.
But the green tech area is obviously appealing to us as well as possible growth.
It became appealing to me when I had a grandson because I realized that I wanted to have better stories to tell him about the role that I played in making it a safer planet.
And that window is, you know, is narrowing.
And I know the current trend in the USA is, you know, it's going back to fossil fuels and so on.
But I think, you know, when Trump goes away, that there'll be a massive reality check to fall in line with the rest of the world in terms of policy.
So, so I'm confident that that shift in public will come around, but I'm just not sure when I agree.

I think there must be a lot of people like us just kind of holding their breath for the next three years and hoping that things get back on the right track, so to speak, in terms of these issues and making progress on them rather than, you know, regressing.
Absolutely.

I think it's interesting that you're in Europe and I wondered like, if you're seeing opportunities there as some, as some of them, you know, there's some windows or doors closed in the U.S. like, do you see opportunities there?

Because I, you know, one of the aspects of Interlex that also we've, we've worked a lot on is in infusing almost all of our work with, with some multicultural dimension to it, you know, and trying to reach diverse audiences and culturally relevant ways.
And my wife and I are avid travelers as well.

And we've all often, when we've gone to Europe, we thought a lot of the multicultural type of work and public awareness, behavior change type of work that we've done over the last 30 years in the US I could so see it being very much embraced in various parts of Europe.
And I'm sure you being there, you see they face a lot of the same problems, challenges, dynamics that the United States has kind of been grappling with for a long time.
And I've always been curious if there'd be opportunities to apply what we do over there in Europe and the uk.
Yeah, I think there's a huge opportunity in terms of cultural exchange from in both directions.
We, we're working with a French company called Madalex that wanted to expand in the US market.
And we've been working with them for three years now.
And we've just set up two or not 15 pilot stores up in upstate New York.

So that's an example of a, a long established European brand that's working in refrigeration management that have a long track record of demonstrating success in a market in a product category that really needs.
Help in the U.S. yeah, I thought that's fascinating.
That actually leads me to.
I was curious to learn more about your current clients.
I saw on the presentation the list of retained clients.

And I was just curious, you know, kind of what the biggest, what the bigger clients are and kind of how from a business perspective, how it's, how that's all working, especially given how you mentioned that what's going on in public health right now.
We also have some university clients where things have also been, you know, kind of slow in terms of funding cuts or entire research teams being kind of, you know, let go.
Currently, we work with NYU on public health research projects, but we have a contract with NYU Medical School, Grossman School of Medicine.
But right now the budget's a lot smaller than what it was a couple years ago.
So I'm just curious to kind of hear about your clients and which ones are really active and kind of what's going on with them.

I did try a couple of full timers a few years ago and I found it led to sort of some inequities in the team if you had full time people and contractors.
So I decided to be bold and just go more into the 1099 route.
And that's been a great success.
It's been.

Obviously it provides you with a flexible workforce, but I found that through Covid, a lot of people were looking for more purpose driven work and really weren't considering ever going back to the office.
You know, they were much happier working remotely with on work that made an impact.
So I think I've been able to use our corporate culture.
I don't like using the word corporate, but let's just say culture as a really active recruiting tool because we just had a little.
We just had two changes recently.
Our creative director, Ali, who'd been with us for years, decided to leave and we'd recruited a graphic designer.
And within six months he had far exceeded what Ali used to produce, both in terms of spirit and verve and design ideas, and had some great software improvements to make as well.
And a similar story with social media Girl who just left about three months ago.
I was lucky to recruit another lady called Jess and she's just been dynamite.
So what I found is that and you, I'm sure you've discovered this in your recruiting journeys too.
Once you identify a very solid, purpose driven organization, it really simplifies things in terms of recruiting.
It certainly simplifies things in terms of client selection.
And I was mobbed by candidates at any openings and I've got a long wait list of people that want to work together.
So that was a very gratifying and humbling experience just to see what strong positioning and how you can benefit from things like recruiting.
So we also use that within our clients to obviously validate the purpose of a good brand is to make those things much more easier.
Because a brand is just a set of values that people want to be around.
So if you can articulate those clearly and bring those to life, then it becomes an easy thing to do.
So the team at the moment is, we've got a core group is me and Eleanor and Claire who are the leadership group.
And then the rest of the seven, I think are all fairly very active, very engaged and really enjoying the work.
We've won quite a few awards this year and last year.
And that tends to excite the team.
And I intend to sort of continue that this year too because I found it's a really good way to get recognition for your work and you know, and shake the team up a bit too.
So they're all 1099 and they're.
Redrock is their main client by more than 50% in every case.
But there are also team members that are active in the arts community and so on.
So their work outside of Red Rock is very complementary to what we do at Red Rock.
And they've all got activities that sort of support and promote the work that we do.
So I actively encourage people, people to have, you know, hobbies and to, to be doing things on the side that really inspires the work.
And I think 1099s are a good way of doing that as well.
Yes, absolutely.
And I think, I think no, you're right.
It's, you know, keeps your overhead low and allows the flexibility.
Like you mentioned, if some of these accounts new account comes in and you can tap more of their time.
But if funding gets cut on something, it's not a huge problem where you have, you're stuck with, you know, carrying overhead, waiting for a new client to sort of ramp up or, or anything.
So I think it's a great model.
We ourselves also, I mean we, we, we have over the years, I mean we always had freelancers obviously, like that's just a mainstay in our industry.
But certainly during COVID and post Covid expanded that, you know, reliance.
We do have FTEs as well, but oftentimes with, like you said, it's the preference now for remote work.

Some of our team members during COVID you know, wanted to become like digital nomads and be able to change their work life balance and went from being full time employees, being freelancers who could then juggle and make their, have better, better choose their time allocation both for themselves, but then also create flexibilities for us right as a business.
So yeah, it can be a great win, win situation.
I mean it sounds to me like, you know, you've got this great team, obviously great reputation, great clients.
You're sort of like quarterback or the quarterback of the team.
And how do you envision your role moving forward?
If you were to decide to, you know, sell the agency, how the agency acquired, how would you see a transition or your role in the future?
I've been stepping back a little bit from the operational work and allowing those that do it much better than I ever did to Actually do what I hired them to do.
That's been a really good little micro experiment because they're all willing and more than capable to take on more responsibility.
So that's been, that's allowed me to be more active in client, you know, in business development.
I'm happy to continue that trend over the next year or two.
Whatever my exit looks like is really just to focus more on business development.
And, you know, I've got to.
I enjoy the.
I enjoy the idea of finding new work and identifying new areas of the business that are in need for me.
That's exciting work.
The, the creative side I'll still keep an eye on, but I find I, I'm probably aging out of that, you know, that spectrum a little bit.
So, yeah, I'd like to see the next two years where I could continue to continue the good work.
You know, I've been investing in, you know, we've got a lot of relationship capital, I guess, in the, in the public health sector.
And, you know, I'm speaking at a conference in Berlin next month and then another one in Tennessee the month after.
So I expect some of those will convert to more work for Red Rock.
I'd like to do more of that going forward.
Just to be traveling and to be articulating what we do and the impact that we have.
And because I find that that gives me a lot of satisfaction and it works.
That's great.
That's great.
That's exciting.

I think maybe then in that case the right union would free you up further to do that kind of sort of that new business development work, that goodwill ambassador work of sharing the philosophy and the success stories with people and in the process, obviously creating opportunities as well.
But that makes sense.
That makes sense.
Very interesting.
Well, any questions you have for me, I know that we'll probably have some after, after this call, and I'm happy to follow up as well.
Have you looked at many other agencies to acquire?
I mean, and what's your, what's your interest?
What's your specific motivation?
Yeah, that's a great question.
I, you know, have been looking.
We actually acquired an agency quite a while ago now.
It was 2012 was the first acquisition that we did.
And we'd been working a lot in healthy, the healthy eating, nutrition and physical activity work.
And in that process, we started getting into that work.
I was mentioning about sugary drink reduction and, and turning down several of those opportunities that had to do with, with that industry.
And I thought, you know, if we're going to be really staking A claim in this, in this, in this public health area around the sugary drinks.
We do something positive too.
And so the agency we acquired was doing a lot of work.
Fresh produce, organic farms, you know, that kind of, that kind of stuff.

And so I thought that'd be kind of an interesting compliment because we were telling people what not to drink and eat and I thought it'd be fun to be able to also spread the word about good things to eat.
It went well.
That agency integrated really well with, with ours.

We still have their largest client on board and, and then over the last two years I'd say I probably I've been looking to see about growth through acquisition primarily because, and you might face this with the public governmental work that we do is always the RFP sort of, you know, boondoggle.

And we've had good luck over the years with RFPs, but the more and more time goes on, you know, recently for example, we, we responded to an RFP and There were like 50 agencies that had responded, you know, so no matter how good you are, your chances in A, in a 50 agency RFP is, are not going to be great unless you're already pre selected, you know, as sometimes happen.

So I thought, you know, it's, we're not, we're continuing those kind of efforts, but I just thought growth through acquisition might be a great way for a mature company like ours to make some growth happen rather than leave it so much of it to chance, you know, year to year.
So I probably looked closely and had conversations maybe with, I mean it's not a lot really.
I'd say five, maybe five, I mean as far as actual conversations, maybe about five different agencies that I've, that I've chatted with over the last two years.
Primarily because there's not a lot of agencies out there like ours, as you know, that, that are a good mission fit.

And so there have been a handful that I've seen that were in some cases, but none of them have really panned out in terms of an acquisition because of the different circumstances, you know, and in one case we were really excited about an agency and we were one of several suitors.
It was a New York City based agency that did branding work for large nonprofits, very really cool, Brooklyn based and purpose driven.
And unfortunately we made an offer, but unfortunately somebody made a better offer, you know, and we just got beat out.
So it's just an ongoing process for me.
Try to find the right opportunity and the right fit.
And it has to be like, like you said, it has to be the mission.
A mission fit, you know, and then, of course, in the end, it has to be also a good financial fit for both seller and buyer.
Are you.
Are we in the right space financially, from what you've seen?
I know the financials I've disclosed aren't detailed, but they're still quite instructive.
Yes, I mean, I think.
I think.
I think so.

You know, in the sense that definitely there have been some agents, a couple agencies that I've looked at that were losing money, you know, although they had the right mission fit and they had, you know, good teams and good clients.
But for whatever reason, maybe they had overextended their overhead.
They were.

You know, I think something that happens maybe is that, I mean, we've gone through this when you work with people for a long time, you know, and maybe there are flush times and you grow, and then it's really hard to streamline, hard to get back to within living within your means as a business.
And so I ran into a couple likelihoods where acquiring them would have meant immediately having to lay off a bunch of people.
And, you know, who really wants to do that?
So, in fact, like, the way that you created this structure with the way you have your team structured as 1099s, as you said, and the fact that you're profitable, I think those are great.
I mean, that's.
That's hats off to you because it's.

They might have been thinking of it as an investment towards the future and towards growth, and that's understandable, you know, so.
But it's hard to come in and have to turn the ship around.
Yeah, no, I wouldn't.
I wouldn't wish that on anyone.
And it's not really.

Because I'm.

We.

And transparency and trust are very highly regarded.
And it's just been great making that.
